abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

islamic-golden-age.name: Islamic Golden Age
islamic-golden-age.summary: A period of cultural flourishing in Islamic history from the 8th to 14th century, beginning with Baghdad's House of Wisdom under Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid and ending with the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

ibn-sayyar-al-warraq.name: Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq
ibn-sayyar-al-warraq.summary: An Iraqi author from Baghdad who compiled the tenth-century Kitab al-Tabikh, the earliest known Arabic cookbook, containing over 600 recipes.

nawal-nasrallah.name: Nawal Nasrallah
nawal-nasrallah.summary: A U.S.-based Iraqi food writer and translator known for her cookbook on Iraqi cuisine and for annotated English translations of medieval Arabic cookbooks, including the Abbasid-era Kitab al-Tabikh.

arab-american-national-museum.name: Arab American National Museum
arab-american-national-museum.summary: Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, established in 2005 as the first and largest in the world devoted to Arab American history and culture.

ibn-al-faqih.name: Ibn al-Faqih
ibn-al-faqih.summary: A 10th-century Persian historian and geographer, active around 902, famous for his concise geographical work on lands, written in Arabic.

umayyad-mosque.name: Umayyad Mosque
umayyad-mosque.summary: Great Mosque of Damascus, one of the oldest and largest mosques in the world, built on a site used for worship since the Iron Age; tradition holds it contains the head of John the Baptist.

al-walid-i.name: Al-Walid I
al-walid-i.summary: Sixth Umayyad caliph (705–715) who expanded the caliphate to its largest extent and built major mosques including the Great Mosque of Damascus.

john-the-baptist.name: John the Baptist
john-the-baptist.summary: Itinerant Jewish preacher active near the Jordan River (c. 6 BC–AD 30), revered in Christianity and Islam (as Yahya ibn Zakariya) as a forerunner of Jesus.

great-mosque-of-samarra.name: Great Mosque of Samarra
great-mosque-of-samarra.summary: A former congregational mosque in Samarra, Iraq, commissioned in 848 CE and completed in 851 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil; it was the world's largest mosque at the time.

al-mutawakkil.name: al-Mutawakkil
al-mutawakkil.summary: Tenth Abbasid caliph, ruling from 847 until his assassination in 861, remembered as devoutly religious and a prolific builder whose caliphate reached its greatest territorial extent.

umayyad-architecture.name: Umayyad architecture
umayyad-architecture.summary: Architectural style developed under the Umayyad Caliphate (661 to 750), mainly in Syria, blending Byzantine and Sasanian influences and introducing features such as the mihrab to mosques.

mihrab.name: Mihrab
mihrab.summary: A niche in a mosque's wall marking the qibla, the direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims face when praying.

dome-of-the-rock.name: Dome of the Rock
dome-of-the-rock.summary: Octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, the world's oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture, built in 691 to 692 CE on the orders of Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik.

abd-al-malik-ibn-marwan.name: Abd al-Malik
abd-al-malik-ibn-marwan.summary: The fifth Umayyad caliph, ruling from 685 to 705, who reunited the Caliphate after civil war and fought renewed wars with the Byzantine Empire.

muhammad.name: Muhammad
muhammad.summary: The founder of Islam, born around 570 CE in Mecca, whom Muslims believe received revelations from God beginning around 610 as the final prophet.

qusayr-amra.name: Qusayr 'Amra
qusayr-amra.summary: A well-preserved desert castle in present-day Jordan, built between 723 and 743 by the future Umayyad caliph Walid II, notable for its early Islamic frescoes and UNESCO World Heritage status.

al-walid-ii.name: Al-Walid II
al-walid-ii.summary: Eleventh Umayyad caliph, ruling from 743 until his assassination in 744, having succeeded his uncle Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik.

mshatta.name: Mshatta
mshatta.summary: The ruin of an Umayyad winter palace near Amman, Jordan, probably commissioned by Caliph Al-Walid II around 743–744; its ornate facade is now in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.

copts.name: Copts
copts.summary: A Christian ethnoreligious group native to Egypt, descended from the ancient Egyptians, historically speaking the Coptic language and now the largest Christian population in the Middle East.

al-ma-mun.name: Al-Ma'mun
al-ma-mun.summary: Seventh Abbasid caliph (786-833) who promoted the translation movement and flowering of science in Baghdad, during whose reign al-Khwarizmi's algebra text was published.

four-centred-arch.name: Four-centred arch
four-centred-arch.summary: A low, wide, pointed arch shape, including the moderately depressed Persian arch of Islamic architecture and the flatter Tudor arch of English architecture.

samarra.name: Samarra
samarra.summary: A city on the Tigris in Iraq, founded in 836 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim as a new capital and military base; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

ziggurat.name: Ziggurat
ziggurat.summary: A massive terraced structure built in ancient Mesopotamia and Iran, believed by the Sumerians to house the gods, with the Great Ziggurat of Ur among the best known examples.

oleg-grabar.name: Oleg Grabar
oleg-grabar.summary: French-born art historian and archeologist (1929–2011) who became a leading figure in the study of Islamic art and architecture in the West.

jonathan-m-bloom.name: Jonathan Bloom
jonathan-m-bloom.summary: American art historian (born 1950), Norma Jean Calderwood University Professor of Islamic and Asian Art at Boston College.

byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628.name: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628
byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628.summary: A 26-year war, the last and most devastating of the Roman–Persian wars, in which Heraclius eventually reversed major Persian gains, but both empires were left exhausted.

khosrow-ii.name: Khosrow II
khosrow-ii.summary: Last great pre-Islamic monarch of Iran, ruling the Sasanian Empire from 590 to 628; he conquered Roman territory in the Middle East before being deposed and killed by his own son.

maurice-emperor.name: Maurice
maurice-emperor.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 582 to 602 and the last of the Justinian dynasty, a successful general who ended the war with Persia and campaigned extensively against the Avars in the Balkans; he lived 539–602.

arab-conquest-of-mesopotamia.name: Arab conquest of Mesopotamia
arab-conquest-of-mesopotamia.summary: A Rashidun Caliphate campaign from 633 to 638 AD that ended Sasanian control of Mesopotamia, the first time the region was ruled by Semitic-speaking people since 539 BC.

rashidun-caliphate.name: Rashidun Caliphate
rashidun-caliphate.summary: Early Islamic state (632–661 CE) led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad's death, which rapidly expanded into the dominant power of West Asia and North Africa.

neo-babylonian-empire.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
neo-babylonian-empire.summary: The last empire ruled by native Mesopotamian kings, from 626 to 539 BC, remembered for Nebuchadnezzar II's destruction of Jerusalem's Temple and a cultural renaissance in Babylon.

heraclius.name: Heraclius
heraclius.summary: Byzantine emperor from 610 to 641 who seized power in a revolt against Phocas, then fought long wars against Persia and the Arabs, driving the Persians from Asia Minor before losing territory to Arab conquests.

legio-iii-cyrenaica.name: Legio III Cyrenaica
legio-iii-cyrenaica.summary: A Roman legion originating under Mark Antony, later stationed in Egypt and Arabia Petraea, fighting campaigns against Nubians and Jews, with records into the 5th century.

bosra.name: Bostra
bosra.summary: Ancient city in southern Syria, the northern capital of the Nabataean kingdom and later a prosperous Roman provincial capital; today a UNESCO World Heritage archaeological site.

umar.name: Umar
umar.summary: Second Rashidun caliph, ruling 634 to 644; a close companion of Muhammad whose conquests brought Persia and much of the Byzantine Empire under Muslim rule before his assassination.

g-kt-rks.name: Göktürks
g-kt-rks.summary: A Turkic people of medieval Inner Asia who, under Bumin Qaghan and his sons, overthrew the Rouran Khaganate and founded the First Turkic Khaganate in the 6th century.

battle-of-nineveh-627.name: Battle of Nineveh (627)
battle-of-nineveh-627.summary: The climactic 627 battle of the Byzantine-Sasanian War, in which Emperor Heraclius's forces defeated and killed the Persian commander Rhahzadh, later triggering civil war in Persia and weakening the Sasanian Empire.

rhahzadh.name: Rhahzadh
rhahzadh.summary: A Sasanian general of Armenian origin, known in Byzantine sources as Rhazates, who served under Shah Khosrow II.

anastasian-war.name: Anastasian War
anastasian-war.summary: A war fought from 502 to 506 between the Byzantine and Sasanian Empires, the first major conflict between them since 440 and a prelude to a century of further wars.

anastasius-i-dicorus.name: Anastasius I
anastasius-i-dicorus.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 491 to 518 who came to the throne at 61 and enacted lasting financial and administrative reforms that strengthened the empire for successors including Justinian I.

nusaybin.name: Nisibis
nusaybin.summary: An ancient city in northern Mesopotamia held in turn by Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids, Romans and Sasanians, and made capital of Roman Mesopotamia after a treaty in 298 CE.

yazdegerd-iii.name: Yazdegerd III
yazdegerd-iii.summary: The last Sasanian King of Kings (632-651), enthroned at age eight, whose defeats by the Rashidun Caliphate ended over four centuries of pre-Islamic Iranian rule; killed near Merv in 651.

kavad-ii.name: Kavad II
kavad-ii.summary: Sasanian King of Kings of Iran briefly in 628, who overthrew and executed his father Khosrow II and made peace with the Byzantines, ending their long war.

true-cross.name: True Cross
true-cross.summary: In Christian tradition, the original wooden cross on which Jesus was crucified, said to have been recovered in Jerusalem by Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, around 326–328.

phocas.name: Phocas
phocas.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 602 to 610 who rose from the army to overthrow Emperor Maurice, and was himself overthrown and executed by Heraclius.

narses.name: Narses
narses.summary: A Roman general and statesman of Armenian heritage (c. 478–573) who helped reconquer Italy for Emperor Justinian I, defeating the Ostrogoths at Taginae in 552 and Mons Lactarius in 553.

muslim-conquest-of-syria.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid
muslim-conquest-of-syria.summary: The most important commander of the Rashidun army during the Muslim conquest of Byzantine Syria, fought between 634 and 638 CE.

abu-ubayd-al-thaqafi.name: Abu Ubaid al-Thaqafi
abu-ubayd-al-thaqafi.summary: Commander in the Rashidun Caliphate's army from Ta'if who took charge of Muslim forces against the Sasanians but was killed by a war elephant at the Battle of the Bridge.

battle-of-the-bridge.name: Battle of the Bridge
battle-of-the-bridge.summary: A 634 CE clash on the Euphrates where Persian Sasanian forces under Bahman Jaduya defeated the invading Arab Muslim army of Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi, the Sasanians' only major victory over the Rashidun Caliphate.

al-muthanna-ibn-haritha.name: al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
al-muthanna-ibn-haritha.summary: A Muslim Arab general in the army of the Rashidun Caliphate.

battle-of-buwaib.name: Battle of Buwaib
battle-of-buwaib.summary: A battle fought soon after the Battle of the Bridge, in which the Rashidun Caliphate's Muslim forces defeated the Sassanid Persian army.

majlis-al-shura.name: Majlis al-Shura
majlis-al-shura.summary: Arab advisory or consultative council; in Islamic tradition, one of two ways a caliph could be chosen, the other being nomination.

sa-d-ibn-abi-waqqas.name: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
sa-d-ibn-abi-waqqas.summary: An Arab Muslim commander and companion of Muhammad who founded the city of Kufa and led the Muslim conquest of Persia.

syriac-language.name: Syriac language
syriac-language.summary: An Eastern Aramaic dialect that emerged around the 1st century AD and became the main literary and liturgical language of Syriac Christian communities.

edessa.name: Edessa
edessa.summary: An ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia (modern Şanlıurfa, Turkey) founded by Seleucus I Nicator, later capital of the Kingdom of Osroene and, during the Crusades, of the County of Edessa.

tel-rehov.name: Tel Rehov
tel-rehov.summary: An archaeological site in Israel's Jordan Valley occupied in the Bronze and Iron Ages, later home to a synagogue with one of the longest Jewish inscriptions from late antiquity.

church-of-the-east.name: Church of the East
church-of-the-east.summary: An Eastern Christian branch, also called the Nestorian Church, that arose from 5th-century Christological disputes and originated in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire.

miaphysitism.name: Miaphysitism
miaphysitism.summary: A Christian doctrine holding that Jesus is fully divine and fully human in a single nature, held by the Oriental Orthodox Churches in contrast to the two-nature view set at Chalcedon in 451.

council-of-chalcedon.name: Council of Chalcedon
council-of-chalcedon.summary: The fourth ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 451 CE, which declared Jesus fully divine and fully human, rejecting rival views that saw him as only divine or as having separate natures.

suru.name: Serugh (Suruç)
suru.summary: The Syriac name (Sruḡ) for Suruç, a town now in Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey, near the Syrian border and inhabited today mainly by Kurds.

manbij.name: Manbij
manbij.summary: A city in northern Syria near the Euphrates, historically known as Mabbug, whose population practices Naqshbandi Sufism and which has changed hands repeatedly during the Syrian civil war since 2012.

al-mansur.name: Al-Mansur
al-mansur.summary: Second Abbasid caliph (714-775) who founded the round city that became the core of Baghdad and is regarded by historians as the true founder of the Abbasid Caliphate.

house-of-wisdom.name: House of Wisdom
house-of-wisdom.summary: A major Abbasid-era library and academy in Baghdad, founded under caliphs in the 8th century and turned into a public center of scholarship, destroyed in the Mongol siege of 1258.

harun-al-rashid.name: Harun al-Rashid
harun-al-rashid.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph, reigning 786 to 809, whose rule is traditionally seen as the start of the Islamic Golden Age; he founded the House of Wisdom library in Baghdad.

hunayn-ibn-ishaq.name: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
hunayn-ibn-ishaq.summary: An Iraqi Arab Nestorian scholar and physician (808-873) who was the era's most productive translator of Greek medical and scientific texts into Arabic and Syriac, earning the title 'Sheikh of the Translators.'

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

ban-m-s-brothers.name: Banū Mūsā brothers
ban-m-s-brothers.summary: Three Persian polymath brothers active in 9th-century Baghdad's House of Wisdom, who translated Greek works and made advances in geometry and astronomy.

book-of-ingenious-devices.name: Book of Ingenious Devices
book-of-ingenious-devices.summary: An illustrated work on mechanical devices and automata published in 850 by the Banū Mūsā brothers at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, describing about one hundred inventions.

al-kindi.name: Al-Kindi
al-kindi.summary: A Mesopotamian Arab polymath (c. 801-873) hailed as the 'father of Arab philosophy,' who oversaw the translation of Greek texts at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and wrote on subjects from mathematics to medicine.

al-khwarizmi.name: Al-Khwarizmi
al-khwarizmi.summary: A mathematician, astronomer and geographer (c. 780-850) of the Islamic Golden Age who worked at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and is regarded as the father of algebra.

al-jabr.name: Al-Jabr
al-jabr.summary: An early ninth-century Arabic mathematical treatise by al-Khwarizmi that gave algebra its name and provided the first systematic method for solving polynomial equations.

th-bit-ibn-qurra.name: Thābit ibn Qurra
th-bit-ibn-qurra.summary: Pagan Sabian scholar (826 or 836–901) active in Abbasid Baghdad who made major discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine.

harran.name: Harran
harran.summary: Ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia, founded between the 25th and 20th centuries BC, a major religious centre devoted to the moon god Sin and site of the 53 BC Battle of Carrhae.

ismail-al-jazari.name: al-Jazari
ismail-al-jazari.summary: Polymath and mechanical engineer in Mesopotamia (1136-1206) who wrote a 1206 book describing 50 mechanical devices, including the famous elephant clock, earning him the title 'father of robotics'.

al-khalil-ibn-ahmad-al-farahidi.name: Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi
al-khalil-ibn-ahmad-al-farahidi.summary: An eighth-century Arab philologist and lexicographer (718-786) from Basra who compiled the first Arabic dictionary and introduced the standard vowel-mark system, and pioneered cryptography.

frequency-analysis.name: Frequency analysis
frequency-analysis.summary: A cryptanalysis technique that studies how often letters and letter combinations appear in a text, used to break classical ciphers.

al-mu-tadid.name: al-Mu'tadid
al-mu-tadid.summary: Abbasid caliph from 892 to 902, considered the dynasty's most militarily active ruler, who recovered lost provinces and restored much of the caliphate's power.

jabir-ibn-hayyan.name: Jabir ibn Hayyan
jabir-ibn-hayyan.summary: Purported author (died c. 806–816) of a vast body of Arabic works on alchemy, chemistry, and Shi'ite philosophy, known for an early theory linking sulfur and mercury to metals.

umayyad-caliphate.name: Umayyad Caliphate
umayyad-caliphate.summary: Second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 661 to 750 from its capital Damascus; expanded Muslim rule across the Maghreb, Iberia, Central Asia and Sindh.

al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf.name: Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf.summary: A governor (c. 658-714) who served the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling Iraq and the east under two caliphs and instituting reforms such as making Arabic the language of Iraq's tax registers.

numayrid-dynasty.name: Numayrid dynasty
numayrid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty ruling parts of Upper Mesopotamia from 990, controlling cities like Harran and Raqqa until the Seljuk conquest in the late 11th century; emir Mani' ibn Shabib later fortified Harran as his palace.

hamdanid-dynasty.name: Hamdanid dynasty
hamdanid-dynasty.summary: A Shia Muslim Arab dynasty descended from the Banu Taghlib tribe that ruled Upper Mesopotamia and Syria from 890 to 1004.

sayf-al-dawla.name: Sayf al-Dawla
sayf-al-dawla.summary: Founder of the Emirate of Aleppo in northern Syria (916–967), who turned to Syria after a failed attempt with his brother to control Baghdad in the early 940s, known for leading raids against a resurgent Byzantine Empire in the Arab–Byzantine wars.

upper-mesopotamia.name: Upper Mesopotamia
upper-mesopotamia.summary: The uplands and plain of northwestern Iraq, northeastern Syria and southeastern Turkey, known since the 7th century as al-Jazira, 'the island,' between the Tigris and Euphrates.

qarmatians.name: Qarmatians
qarmatians.summary: An Isma'ili Shia militant movement centred in eastern Arabia from 899 CE, notorious for sacking Mecca in 930 CE and stealing the Black Stone.

ibn-al-adim.name: Ibn al-Adim
ibn-al-adim.summary: An Arab biographer and historian from Aleppo (1192–1262), best known for his multi-volume history of Aleppo's famous men and a shorter chronicle version of the same work.

clifford-edmund-bosworth.name: Clifford Edmund Bosworth
clifford-edmund-bosworth.summary: English historian and Orientalist (1928–2015) specializing in Arabic and Iranian studies.

ibn-hawqal.name: Ibn Hawqal
ibn-hawqal.summary: A 10th-century Arab geographer and chronicler who traveled widely from 943 to 969 and wrote 'The Face of the Earth,' completed in 977.

syriac-orthodox-church.name: Syriac Orthodox Church
syriac-orthodox-church.summary: An Oriental Orthodox church, also known as the Jacobite Church, tracing its origins to the ancient Church of Antioch and led by the Patriarch of Antioch.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

geonim.name: Geonim
geonim.summary: Chiefs of the Sura and Pumbedita Talmudic academies in Babylonia under the Abbasid Caliphate, generally accepted as the Jewish community's spiritual leaders in the Early Middle Ages.

kabbalah.name: Kabbalah
kabbalah.summary: Esoteric school of Jewish mysticism forming the basis of mystical interpretation of Jewish scripture, emerging in 12th-13th century Occitania.

amr-ibn-ubayd.name: Amr ibn Ubayd
amr-ibn-ubayd.summary: An early leader of the rationalist Mu'tazila theological movement and student of Hasan al-Basri, who led the movement in the early Abbasid period until his death in 761.

al-tabari.name: Al-Tabari
al-tabari.summary: A Sunni Muslim polymath and historian (839–923) from Tabaristan, Persia, famous for his Quranic commentary and historical chronicle.

history-of-the-prophets-and-kings.name: History of the Prophets and Kings
history-of-the-prophets-and-kings.summary: A world history completed in 915 AD by the Muslim historian al-Tabari, tracing events from creation to the Abbasid era and considered one of the most important sources for early Islamic history.
history-of-the-prophets-and-kings.source_title: History of the Prophets and Kings

nimrod.name: Nimrod
nimrod.summary: Biblical figure in Genesis described as a mighty hunter and king in Shinar, later traditions linking him to the Tower of Babel, though no historical record of him has been found.

nabataeans-of-iraq.name: Nabataeans of Iraq
nabataeans-of-iraq.summary: A name medieval Islamic scholars used for the rural, Aramaic-speaking native inhabitants of central and southern Iraq from the 7th to 10th centuries, distinct from the ancient Nabataeans of Petra.

asoristan.name: Asoristan
asoristan.summary: The Sasanian Empire's province covering Assyria and Babylonia from 226 to 637 CE, dissolved after the Arab Muslim conquest of Persia.

mandaeans.name: Mandaeans
mandaeans.summary: An ethnoreligious group following Mandaeism who regard John the Baptist as their final prophet and are among the earliest practitioners of baptism, with their numbers sharply declining since the 2003 Iraq war.

tur-abdin.name: Tur Abdin
tur-abdin.summary: A hilly region in southeastern Turkey between the Tigris and the Syrian border, a historic Christian monastic heartland for the Syriac Orthodox, with monasteries dating to the 6th century.

alawites.name: Alawites
alawites.summary: Ethnoreligious group following Alawism, an offshoot of Shia Islam founded in the 9th century, living mainly in Syria and parts of the Levant.

al-khasibi.name: Al-Khasibi
al-khasibi.summary: A ninth- and tenth-century religious leader and missionary (873-968) who played a central role in developing the Alawite sect in Iraq and Syria.

twelver-shi-ism.name: Twelver Shi'ism
twelver-shi-ism.summary: The largest branch of Shia Islam, holding that twelve divinely appointed Imams beginning with Ali succeeded the prophet Muhammad, with the twelfth expected to return as the Mahdi.

ibn-wahshiyya.name: Ibn Wahshiyya
ibn-wahshiyya.summary: An Iraqi Aramaic-speaking agriculturalist, toxicologist and alchemist who died around 930, best known for his influential Arabic work on agriculture, astrology and magic.

sennacherib.name: Sennacherib
sennacherib.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BC, famed in the Hebrew Bible for his Levant campaign, who destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and expanded the capital Nineveh.

sabians.name: Sabians
sabians.summary: A religious group named in the Quran whose true identity is uncertain; the name was later claimed by groups such as the star-worshipping Sabians of Harran.
